context: Use a deterministic college-savings calculation with no external data source; all figures are integer cents and all rates are integer basis points (100 bps = 1%). Null rates would default to 500 bps nominal return and 400 bps college-cost inflation, but this input supplies 1200 bps and 0 bps instead. A family has 5000 cents saved, enrollment is 1 month away (so exactly 1 month-end deposit is allowed before the first bill), the annual all-in college cost in today's money is 10000 cents, and college lasts 3 years. No monthly budget was supplied. Each month: first add investment growth to the opening balance, rounded to the nearest cent with ties away from zero, using the annual rate divided by 12; then make the deposit if the month is within the saving window; then pay the annual bill if one is due. College costs inflate only at 12-month anniversaries from today, each increase rounded separately to cents; with enrollment at month 1, bills occur at months 1, 13, and 25, and contributions stop after the month-1 deposit. Savings keep earning returns during college. The projection ends immediately after the final bill; any negative balance at a bill means that contribution fails, and later gains cannot repair it. Find the smallest whole-cent fixed monthly contribution that funds every bill. Without a budget, the affordability fields (fits_monthly_budget and monthly_budget_shortfall_cents) stay null.
